top.line: A custom Firefox is feasible; maintaining it is costly
top.para: The plan builds a custom Firefox with a Ruflo hive, an sgit vault and a behaviour policy, using the least invasive layer first, then a patch set. The iPad needs a fork of the Swift codebase. With 26 releases a year on two codebases, Mozilla should sell maintenance to one person, about 50p a release.

in-short.line: Lowest layer first; maintenance is the real cost
in-short.para: The goal is a Firefox that behaves as I want on laptop and iPad, next month and next year. Policies, preferences, CSS and an extension come before a renamed front-end patch set. The iPad is a second codebase, and Mozilla already sells customisation to organisations but not to one person.

want.line: The aim is a Firefox that stays mine
want.para: Version one is affordable; what matters is that it does not break afterwards. The workflow from the agentics talk is reused: a Ruflo hive of Claude Code workers, an sgit vault as memory and an Agent Behaviour Policy as mandate. The plan is a proposal and has not yet been run.

brief.line: The brief is my wants, triaged by layer
brief.para: Explorer coding starts with my own words: compact density, a hiding toolbar on the iPad, no sponsored content or unused AI features, my search engine, my own new-tab page and a daily-tools sidebar. The first worker finds the lowest layer for each want, since every layer up costs more maintenance.

layers.line: Most of the list needs no fork at all
layers.para: Enterprise policies in policies.json survive updates and cover menus, search, new-tab and the AI chatbot sidebar, and locked hidden preferences enable userChrome.css, the most powerful but least stable layer. An unlisted, Mozilla-signed extension handles sidebars, buttons and new-tab pages. The hive writes all four with tests.

fork.line: A small renamed patch set covers the rest
fork.para: Firefox's code is on GitHub since 2025, and a personal fork is a patch set on each release, as LibreWolf carries 63 patches and Debian 17. Artifact mode skips the C++ compile for interface changes. Mozilla's trademark policy means a modified build cannot be distributed as Firefox.

ipad.line: The iPad needs a fork of Firefox's Swift codebase
ipad.para: Apple's guideline 2.5.6 requires WebKit outside the EU and Japan, and Mozilla will not build Gecko for iOS. Firefox for iOS is a separate open-source Swift codebase, so the only route is a fork built in Xcode. A free Apple account install lasts 7 days; a paid account gives a year.

loop.line: Keeping it working means following 26 releases a year
loop.para: Since Firefox 155 a major release ships every two weeks, on each of two codebases; LibreWolf ships within three days with a team. On each release the hive rebases, builds, tests and reports into the vault, under a policy barring security or trademark changes. PortGPT reported 89.15% success, but a person still approves every release.

business.line: Mozilla should sell customisation maintenance to one person
business.para: Only Mozilla can ship a modified build called Firefox, and it already sells Firefox Enterprise and custom development to organisations. A personal offer would be: explore free, keep a customisation working for about 50p a release, or £13 a year, adopt a change for £50 to £500, or own a branded build by contract.

limits.line: The plan is unrun and the prices are illustrative
limits.para: Every step was checked against documentation, not tried end to end. The prices are mine, not Mozilla's, and its consumer offer does not exist while enterprise prices are not public. A person approves every release, and the iPad route needs a developer account and is limited to WebKit.
